questions.stem: How does the endocrine system differ from the nervous system in the way it regulates the body?
questions.why: The endocrine system is slow, reads the blood, and is paired with the nervous system. It sends hormones throughout the body to maintain homeostasis.

options.t: It acts only upon the skeletal muscles
options.why: It acts on organs, glands, and tissues broadly.

options.t: It is slow and works through the blood
It works only during rest and digestion
options.why: It operates continuously, not only at rest.

options.t: It is fast and works through nerve fibers
options.why: That describes the nervous system.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a chemical messenger the body uses for intercellular communication?
questions.why: Chemical messengers include neurotransmitters, hormones, ions, growth factors, and products of cellular metabolism. Most act on receptors that stimulate a target response.

options.why: Those are structural proteins.
Those are cell fragments for clotting.
Those are red blood cells.

questions.stem: How do steroid and nonsteroidal hormones differ in how they reach their target?
questions.why: Steroid hormones diffuse straight through the cell membrane. Nonsteroidal hormones cannot, so they bind to receptors in the membrane instead.

options.t: Steroids act on glands; nonsteroids on muscle
options.why: Both act on many tissue types.

options.t: Steroids bind the membrane; nonsteroids cross it
options.why: The two are reversed here.

options.t: Steroids travel in lymph; nonsteroids in blood
options.why: Both travel in the bloodstream.

options.t: Steroids cross the membrane; nonsteroids bind it

questions.stem: What is the difference between an agonist and an antagonist?
questions.why: Agonists trigger a cell to produce an action; antagonists block the action of agonists. Both are ways hormones increase or decrease the rate of cellular metabolism — and the same terms describe how many of your drugs work.

options.t: Agonists trigger an action; antagonists block it
Agonists block a receptor; antagonists activate it
options.why: The two are reversed here.

options.t: Agonists act on steroids; antagonists on peptides
options.why: Both terms apply to any hormone type.

options.t: Agonists raise metabolism; antagonists raise growth
options.why: Both can raise or lower a given process.

questions.stem: Why is the pituitary gland called the master gland?
questions.why: The pituitary is the major endocrine gland — the master gland. Found in the brain, this pea-shaped gland's secretions control those of the other endocrine glands.

options.t: Its output controls the other glands
It is the largest gland in the body
options.why: It is small, roughly pea-sized.
The hypothalamus regulates the pituitary, not the reverse.

options.t: It makes more hormones than any gland
options.why: Hormone count is not what earns the title.

questions.stem: What is the most important role of the hypothalamus?
questions.why: The hypothalamus regulates the function of the pituitary gland, and most importantly it links the neuro and endocrine systems through it.

options.t: It clears hormones once they have acted
options.why: Clearance happens in the liver and kidneys.
Most hormones come from the target glands themselves.

options.t: It links the nervous and endocrine systems
It stores hormones until they are needed
options.why: The posterior pituitary stores certain hormones.

questions.stem: The thyroid gland is stimulated by the release of which hormone, and from where?
questions.why: The thyroid is stimulated by TSH from the pituitary gland, and it sits in a negative feedback loop with the anterior pituitary.

options.why: Calcitonin comes from the thyroid itself.
ACTH targets the adrenal cortex.
PTH comes from the parathyroids.

questions.stem: Calcitonin, secreted by the thyroid, has what effect on blood calcium?
questions.why: Calcitonin from the thyroid LOWERS blood calcium. Parathyroid hormone does the opposite — it INCREASES blood calcium. Two glands, opposite jobs.

options.t: It has no effect on calcium, only on metabolism
options.why: Calcitonin acts specifically on calcium.
That is parathyroid hormone's effect.
Calcium is not converted into another element.

questions.stem: What do the parathyroid glands secrete, and what does it do?
questions.why: Parathyroid glands secrete parathyroid hormone to INCREASE blood calcium levels — the counterweight to the thyroid's calcitonin.

options.why: That comes from the pituitary.
That is the thyroid's secretion and the opposite effect.

options.t: T3 and T4, regulating metabolic rate
options.why: Those govern metabolism, not calcium.

questions.stem: TSH stimulates production of hormones that play a role in which three processes?
questions.why: TSH stimulates the production and secretion of T3 and T4, which play roles in growth, development, and metabolism.

options.why: Those are immune and hematologic processes.
Those are governed by other hormones.
Those are digestive processes.

questions.stem: The pancreas is unusual among the glands in what way?
questions.why: The pancreas is an organ with both endocrine functions (releasing into the blood) and exocrine functions (producing digestive juices).

options.t: It has both endocrine and exocrine functions
It responds only to nervous stimulation, not hormonal
options.why: It responds to blood glucose levels directly.

options.t: It is the only gland located outside the abdomen
options.why: It sits within the abdomen.

options.t: It produces no hormones of its own
options.why: It produces insulin, glucagon, and somatostatin.

questions.stem: Which pancreatic cells secrete glucagon, and what does it do?
questions.why: Alpha cells secrete glucagon, which stimulates the liver to convert glycogen — stored primarily in the liver and skeletal muscle — into glucose.

options.t: Beta cells; insulin drives glucose into cells
options.why: Those secrete insulin, which lowers glucose.

options.t: Alpha cells; glucagon frees stored glycogen
F cells; pancreatic polypeptide is released
options.why: Those secrete pancreatic polypeptide.
Those secrete somatostatin.

questions.stem: Beta cells secrete insulin in response to what, and what does insulin cause?
questions.why: Beta cells secrete insulin in response to elevated glucose. Insulin causes uptake and metabolism of sugar, fatty acids, and amino acids — driving glucose out of the blood and into cells.

options.t: High glucose; uptake of sugars and fats
Low glucose; release of stored glycogen
options.why: That is glucagon's trigger and action.

options.t: High calcium; uptake of calcium into bone
options.why: Calcium is not the insulin trigger.

options.t: Stress; vasoconstriction and faster heart rate
options.why: That describes the catecholamine response.

questions.stem: Delta cells of the pancreas produce which hormone?
questions.why: Delta cells produce somatostatin, the growth-inhibiting hormone. F cells are the ones producing pancreatic polypeptide.

options.why: That comes from beta cells.
That comes from alpha cells.
That is a digestive enzyme.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of somatostatin preventing both insulin and glucagon?
questions.why: By preventing both insulin and glucagon, somatostatin lets the body avoid wide swings in blood glucose. It is a braking mechanism on both directions at once.

options.t: It shuts the pancreas down during digestion
options.why: It regulates hormone release, not digestion.

options.t: It avoids wide swings in blood glucose
It lets glucose climb freely under stress
options.why: It brakes both directions rather than freeing one.

options.t: It converts free fatty acids into ketones
options.why: That is a function of fat metabolism.

questions.stem: Glucagon stimulates the breakdown of glycogen into glucose. What is that process called, and where does it occur?
questions.why: Glycogenolysis is the breakdown of glycogen to glucose in the liver. Gluconeogenesis is the separate process where glucagon stimulates the liver and kidneys to PRODUCE glucose when required.

options.why: That is making new glucose, not breaking down glycogen.
That is fatty acid breakdown.
That is glucose breakdown for energy.

questions.stem: Where are the adrenal glands located?
questions.why: The adrenal glands sit on top of each kidney. They secrete sex hormones, hormones vital to maintaining water and salt balance, and epinephrine and norepinephrine.

options.t: Behind the stomach alongside the pancreas
options.why: That is the pancreas's location.

options.t: At the base of the neck beside the thyroid
options.why: That is the thyroid's location.

options.t: Within the brain beneath the pituitary
options.why: That is the pineal gland's location.

questions.stem: What effect does cortisol have on blood glucose and the immune system?
questions.why: Cortisol increases blood glucose while promoting insulin resistance, and it suppresses the immune system by preventing T-cell production. It increases with stress and hypoglycemia.

options.why: Cortisol raises glucose and suppresses immunity.
It raises rather than lowers glucose.

options.t: No glucose effect, but boosts T cells
options.why: It does affect glucose, and it suppresses T cells.

questions.stem: Cortisol promotes the retention of which substances, and the excretion of which?
questions.why: Cortisol promotes sodium and water retention from the kidney and small intestine while excreting potassium.

options.t: Retains water only; excretes both sodium and potassium
options.why: Sodium is retained along with the water.

options.t: Retains sodium and water; excretes potassium
Retains potassium; excretes sodium and water
options.why: The two are reversed here.
Calcium and phosphorus are governed by other hormones.

questions.stem: Aldosterone acts on which part of the nephron, and what does it do?
questions.why: Aldosterone drives sodium absorption and potassium secretion by acting on the distal tubules and collecting ducts of the nephron. It is part of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and helps maintain blood pressure.

options.t: Loop of Henle; water reabsorption only
options.why: The loop concentrates urine independently.

options.t: Distal tubules; sodium in, potassium out

options.why: Filtration happens there without aldosterone.
Glucose reabsorption is not aldosterone-driven.

questions.stem: The adrenal medulla produces catecholamines. Which effects do they produce?
questions.why: The adrenal medulla produces adrenaline and noradrenaline — epinephrine and norepinephrine — which raise heart and respiratory rates and blood pressure, cause vasoconstriction, and drive glycogenolysis. All key components of fight-or-flight.

options.why: That is cortisol's effect.

options.t: Slower heart rate and better digestion
options.why: That is the parasympathetic response.
That is aldosterone's effect.

questions.stem: During times of stress, what is the correct hormonal sequence?
questions.why: Hypothalamus, then anterior pituitary releasing ACTH, then adrenal cortex secreting cortisol. Cortisol is a glucocorticoid influencing protein and fat metabolism, controlled by negative feedback.

options.t: Adrenal cortex, then ACTH, then pituitary
options.why: The cortex responds to ACTH rather than releasing it.
The medulla releases catecholamines.

options.t: Pituitary secretes cortisol on its own
options.why: The pituitary releases ACTH, not cortisol.

questions.stem: The adrenal cortex is stimulated to secrete aldosterone under which three conditions?
questions.why: Aldosterone is triggered by a drop in blood pressure or volume, a decrease in sodium level, or an increase in potassium level — all situations where retaining sodium and water helps.

options.t: Low pressure, low sodium, or high potassium

options.why: Those are general stressors, not the specific triggers.

options.t: High pressure, high sodium, or low potassium
options.why: Those are the opposite conditions.

options.t: High glucose, low calcium, or high sodium
options.why: Glucose and calcium do not trigger aldosterone.

questions.stem: The anterior pituitary directs the actions of the ovaries through which two hormones?
questions.why: The anterior pituitary directs the ovaries through follicle stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone.

options.why: Those target the adrenals and thyroid.
Those are produced by the ovaries themselves.
Those act on the uterus and breast.

questions.stem: Which hormone regulates ovulation, the menstrual cycle, and induces labor?
questions.why: Progesterone regulates ovulation and the menstrual cycle and induces labor. Estrogen is responsible for female physical features and reproduction.

options.why: That rises in pregnancy rather than governing the cycle.
That drives female physical characteristics.
That is the primary male sex hormone.

questions.stem: Which hormone increases during pregnancy and is the one detected by a urine pregnancy test?
questions.why: Human chorionic gonadotropin increases during pregnancy — it is the hormone the pee-on-a-stick test looks for.

options.why: That triggers ovulation.
That supports pregnancy but is not the test marker.
That is present throughout the cycle.

questions.stem: Which of the following does testosterone promote?
questions.why: Testosterone promotes healthy sperm production, determines secondary male sex characteristics like voice deepening and facial and pubic hair, stimulates muscle and bone growth, and influences sex drive.

options.why: Those are progesterone's roles.
That is calcitonin's role.
That is aldosterone's role.

questions.stem: The pineal gland synthesizes and secretes which hormone, and what does it affect?
questions.why: The pineal gland is pea-shaped and located in the brain. It synthesizes and secretes melatonin, the hormone affecting sleep-wake patterns.

options.why: That comes from pancreatic delta cells.
That comes from the thyroid.
That comes from the adrenal cortex.

questions.stem: What is the primary function of the lymphatic system?
questions.why: The lymphatic system's primary function is the production, maintenance, and distribution of lymphocytes — a type of white blood cell. It also helps absorb fat, maintain fluid balance, and fight infection.

options.t: Transporting oxygen out to the tissues
options.why: That is a cardiovascular function.
That is an endocrine function.

options.t: Filtering waste products from the blood
options.why: That is a renal function.

questions.stem: How does the lymphatic system prevent tissues from becoming edematous?
questions.why: To prevent tissues from becoming swollen, lymph vessels absorb excess fluid and return it to the central venous circulation.

options.t: The spleen filters excess tissue fluid
options.why: The spleen filters blood, not tissue fluid.

options.t: Lymphocytes pump fluid into the arteries
options.why: Lymph moves by vessel action, not cellular pumping.

options.t: Nodes chemically break down excess fluid
options.why: Nodes filter but do not break fluid down.

options.t: Vessels return excess fluid to the veins

questions.stem: Which white blood cell is the most abundant, and what percentage of WBCs does it make up?
questions.why: Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cell at 40 to 70%. They are made in bone marrow, are the first responders to inflammation, and are the most common cell found in pus.

options.why: Monocytes make up a much smaller share.
Basophils are the least numerous.
That percentage belongs to neutrophils.

questions.stem: Which white blood cell produces swelling that isolates a toxin or disease site, and is also implicated in allergic reactions?
questions.why: Eosinophils, also called acidophiles, produce swelling that isolates a toxin or disease site so it does not spread. That same mechanism can be harmful — the peanut allergy example.

options.why: Those ingest broken-down tissue.
Those attack invaders directly or make antibodies.
Those are first responders to bacterial infection.

questions.stem: Which white blood cell is present in the smallest numbers, and what does it produce?
questions.why: Basophils are the least numerous WBC. They produce heparin, which is critically important in preventing clotting, and they can also consume parasites. A high basophil count suggests a chronic condition.

options.t: Basophils — they produce heparin, which prevents clotting
Eosinophils — they produce histamine, which drives inflammation
options.why: Those isolate toxins and drive allergic swelling.
Lymphocytes do not produce heparin.
Those are the healers that ingest debris.

questions.stem: Which white blood cells are described as the healers that ingest broken-down tissues and cells?
questions.why: Monocytes are the healers. Produced in the bone marrow and regulated continuously, they ingest broken-down tissues and cells.

options.why: Those are the first responders to inflammation.
Those produce heparin and are least numerous.
Those isolate toxins and drive allergy.

questions.stem: Where is the spleen located, and what is its status among lymphatic organs?
questions.why: The spleen is the largest lymphatic organ and sits in the upper left abdominal cavity — which is why left-sided abdominal trauma raises concern for splenic injury.

options.t: The upper left abdominal cavity; it is the smallest lymphatic organ
options.why: It is the largest lymphatic organ, not the smallest.

options.t: The lower left abdominal cavity; it is a secondary lymphoid organ
options.why: It sits in the upper, not lower, quadrant.

options.t: The upper right abdominal cavity; it is the largest lymphatic organ
options.why: The spleen sits on the left.

options.t: The upper left abdominal cavity; it is the largest lymphatic organ

questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of the spleen?
questions.why: The spleen acts as a reservoir for blood reserves, breaks down old RBCs and recycles the iron and hemoglobin, and synthesizes antibodies.

options.t: Producing bile for the digestion of fat
options.why: That is a liver function.
Those are pancreatic functions.

options.t: Storing blood and recycling old red cells

options.why: That is a renal function.

questions.stem: What is the difference between afferent and efferent lymph vessels?
questions.why: Afferent carries lymph TO a node, efferent carries it FROM a node — the same arriving/exiting logic as afferent and efferent nerve pathways.

options.t: Afferent serves limbs; efferent serves trunk
options.why: Both types occur everywhere lymph nodes exist.

options.t: Afferent carries in; efferent carries out
Afferent carries lymph; efferent carries blood
options.why: Both carry lymph, not blood.

options.t: Afferent carries out; efferent carries in
options.why: The two are reversed here.

questions.stem: Lymph ducts drain lymph into which vessels, returning it to general circulation?
questions.why: Lymph ducts drain into one of the subclavian veins, returning lymph to general circulation.

options.why: Lymph joins the venous system at the subclavians first.
Those carry blood from the lungs to the heart.
Those are arteries carrying blood away.

questions.stem: Lymph nodes act as filters for foreign particles including cancer cells. What can they NOT do?
questions.why: Lymph nodes filter foreign particles including cancer cells, but have no detoxification function — they cannot change the structure of what they catch.

options.t: House the B and T cells
options.why: They are major sites of B and T cells.

options.t: Enlarge in the face of disease
options.why: Enlargement is a normal response to disease.
Trapping bacteria is one of their filtering roles.

questions.stem: Lymph nodes are major sites of which cells, and how are they structured?
questions.why: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs and major sites of lymphocytes — B and T cells. Each is enclosed in a fibrous capsule made up of an outer cortex and an inner medulla.

options.t: Red cells and platelets, in a dense capsule
options.why: Those are blood components, not node residents.

options.t: B and T cells, in an outer and inner layer

options.why: Lymphocytes, not macrophages alone, dominate.

options.t: Neutrophils, in an open uncapsuled network
options.why: Nodes are enclosed in a fibrous capsule.

questions.stem: Match each white blood cell to its description.
questions.why: Neutrophils are the most numerous and basophils the least. Eosinophils and basophils are the two tied to allergic response, which matters for anaphylaxis.
pairs: Most abundant at 40–70%; first responders to inflammation; main cell in pus
Produce swelling that isolates a toxin or disease site; involved in allergy
Least numerous; produce heparin to prevent clotting
Go in immediately to assess the problem and attack
The healers; ingest broken-down tissues and cells

questions.stem: Match each endocrine gland to its key hormone or role.
questions.why: Thyroid lowers calcium, parathyroid raises it — the pair most often confused. The pituitary directs, the hypothalamus connects the two control systems.
pairs: The master gland — its secretions control the other endocrine glands
Links the nervous and endocrine systems via the pituitary
Secretes calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium
Secretes parathyroid hormone, which raises blood calcium
Produces epinephrine and norepinephrine for fight-or-flight

questions.stem: Match each pancreatic cell type to what it secretes.
questions.why: Alpha raises glucose, beta lowers it, delta brakes both. Alphabetical order matches the sequence, which makes it easier to hold.
pairs: Insulin — drives uptake of sugar, fatty acids, amino acids
